title: Govt Bigfoot files reveal strange footprints, hoax suspicions and hunters' 'very uneasy feeling'
excerpt: The US Forest Service released three historical files documenting reported encounters involving Bigfoot in Washington state and Montana dating back to the 1940s
content:
The US Forest Service released three historical files documenting reported encounters involving Bigfoot in Washington state and Montana dating back to the 1940s

WASHINGTON, DC: The Trump administration has released three files documenting investigations and reported encounters involving Bigfoot, including an unusual case that dates back more than four decades. The documents were made public by the US Forest Service on October 15 and detail mysterious footprints discovered in Washington state in 1982.

The records include photographs, plaster casts, and a wildlife biologist's findings, along with accounts from people who claimed to have encountered possible Sasquatch tracks. While investigators suspected that some of the footprints were part of an elaborate hoax, one hunter's account described a particularly unsettling experience.

Trump administration releases government files on Bigfoot investigation

The three documents came from the US Forest Service's collection known as the "Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records." One of the most detailed accounts involves an investigation ordered by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) in 1982.

Wildlife biologist Rodney L Johnson was assigned to investigate reported Bigfoot tracks in the Mill Creek Watershed of Washington's Umatilla National Forest. He later documented his findings in a six-page memo to the USDA.

According to Johnson, footprints had been discovered at three separate muddy locations. The tracks measured approximately 15 inches long and 7 inches wide and extended across distances of 25 to 40 feet.

He also noticed signs of disturbance in the thick brush, with vegetation appearing disturbed for another 30 to 40 feet. One footprint had a noticeable "deformation of [the] second toe."

Photographs of some of the tracks were included in the report, while investigators also made plaster casts of several footprints.

Johnson acknowledged that the marks were unusual, writing, "If the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail."

He also noted that some of the markings "would have to be very hard to duplicate" and "appear very natural."

However, despite these observations, the biologist was not convinced that the tracks belonged to Bigfoot.

Wildlife biologist suspects mysterious Bigfoot footprints were a hoax

After examining the evidence, Johnson concluded that the footprints were unlikely to have been made by the large, two-footed creature often described in Bigfoot sightings.

"[I]t is my opinion that the tracks observed … were made by something other than a 300 pound plus two footed being," he wrote.

Johnson also explained why he believed someone could have staged the discovery.

He pointed out that the stride of the footprints did not change even when the tracks moved across different slopes. He also noticed that his own boots sank deeper into the mud than the supposed Bigfoot footprints.

Another detail that raised suspicion was the forest litter surrounding the tracks. Johnson observed that it appeared to have been deliberately brushed aside before the footprints were made.

A US Border Patrol official later shared a similar conclusion in a separate memo sent to the Forest Service office in Walla Walla, Washington.

The official suggested that the tracks were "a very clever attempt to penetrate a hoax," possibly involving the agency to give the discovery greater credibility among the public.

He ultimately believed the footprints were "man made by using some type of soft plaster or rubber coated foot."

Government Bigfoot files include chilling account from Montana hunter

The released records also contain accounts of other reported Bigfoot encounters, including a newspaper clipping from the Clark Fork Valley Press about alleged Sasquatch tracks discovered in Montana in 2003.

Another document is a letter from Leo Kinney, who recalled finding what he believed were Bigfoot tracks during a hunting trip in Montana in the 1940s.

Kinney claimed that he knew other hunters who had come across similar tracks. He also recalled hearing strange noises and noticing an unusual smell during the experience.

According to his account, the group detected a "strong odor" before hearing what he described as "a grunting type noise."

The experience left the hunters unsettled, and Kinney admitted they were not particularly interested in finding out what had made the sounds.

"We were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was, and though we didn’t confess it at this time, in later conversations," he wrote.

Kinney added that the hunters eventually admitted they had all experienced the same feeling.

"We found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs," he recalled.
